title: Grafana dashboards and alerts

story: Monday, 09:10. The weekly spend review opens with a strange number: over the weekend Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, cost almost five times more than usual. The cause takes ten minutes to find. On Friday afternoon a small change put the current time at the top of Nova's instructions, so every model call started with different text, and the prompt cache stopped working. The prompt cache is what lets the model reuse the start of a prompt it has already seen, at a tenth of the normal price, so losing it makes every call expensive.

The painful part is that the numbers showed it from Friday at 18:00. The LLM gateway, our service that every model call passes through, counted every token, and VictoriaMetrics, our metrics database, stored the counts all weekend. Nobody saw them, because nobody opens a database on a Saturday.
hook.question: How do we turn numbers we already store into a screen people actually check, and a message that finds us when nobody is looking?

read.h: A panel is a saved query
p: Grafana is the program that draws the charts. It stores no data of its own: every chart asks a data source, here VictoriaMetrics, a question in PromQL, the query language of Prometheus, and draws the answer. A dashboard is a page of these charts, and each chart is called a panel. A panel has three things: a type, which says how to draw (timeseries for lines, stat for one big number, table), a position on a grid 24 columns wide, and one or more queries, which Grafana calls targets.

Here is the panel that would have caught the weekend. It shows, for each agent, which share of the input tokens came from the cache. The query divides two rates: cache-read tokens per second by all input tokens per second, each summed per agent. When the cache works the share is around 0.9; when it breaks it falls to about 0.15. Thresholds colour the number red under 0.7, so a person who opens the dashboard sees the problem without reading anything.

At the top of the file, templating declares a variable called agent. Grafana shows it as a dropdown filled by label_values, which asks the database which values of the agent label exist. Before Grafana sends a query, it replaces $agent with your choice. When you choose several agents or All, it becomes a pattern such as (nova|cifix), which is why the query matches with =~, the regular-expression matcher, and not with =.

code.text:
{
  "title": "Lab: agent operations",
  "uid": "lab-ops",
  "time": { "from": "now-15m", "to": "now" },
  "templating": { "list": [ {
    "name": "agent", "type": "query", "multi": true, "includeAll": true,
    "datasource": { "type": "prometheus", "uid": "vm" },
    "query": "label_values(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total, agent)" } ] },
  "panels": [
    { "title": "Cache-read share (healthy at 80% or more)", "type": "stat",
      "gridPos": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 8, "h": 8 },
      "fieldConfig": { "defaults": { "unit": "percentunit", "thresholds": { "mode": "absolute", "steps": [
        { "color": "red", "value": null }, { "color": "yellow", "value": 0.7 }, { "color": "green", "value": 0.8 } ] } } },
      "targets": [ { "legendFormat": "{{agent}}",
        "expr": "sum by (agent) (rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{type=\"cache_read\",agent=~\"$agent\"}[1m])) / sum by (agent) (rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{agent=~\"$agent\"}[1m]))" } ] }
  ]
}

notes.text: The uid is the dashboard's address: /d/lab-ops. Links and alert messages point at it, so it never changes after the first release.
A variable named agent: a dropdown with several choices allowed and an All option.
VictoriaMetrics speaks the Prometheus API, so Grafana's normal Prometheus data source type works with it.
stat draws one big number per series. Good for a share you want to read at a glance.
Left third of the first row: 8 of the 24 columns, 8 rows tall.
percentunit: the value is between 0 and 1 and is shown as a percent.
Red below 0.7, yellow from 0.7, green from 0.8.
The ratio of two rates, one per agent. The rates come from counters, the way the previous lesson explained.

p: Some questions are not about numbers but about events: which API errors happened, which tool calls a hook refused. Those records live in VictoriaLogs, and a panel can name that data source instead and query it in LogsQL, its query language. A LogsQL query is a filter, then a pipe, then a step that counts: event.name:api_error agent:~"$agent" | stats by (agent, status_code) count() gives one count per agent and status code over the dashboard's time range.

One panel, one data source: a dashboard can mix metric panels and log panels side by side, because each panel says where its query goes. Before you write any query into a dashboard file, run it in the database's own query page first, because the names there are the real ones.

You can build a dashboard by clicking in Grafana and pressing Save. The trouble starts later: nobody knows who changed a panel or why, a wrong change cannot be reverted, and the dashboard exists only in that one Grafana. So we keep each dashboard as a JSON file in git, and let Grafana read the files. This is called provisioning: Grafana loads dashboards, and data sources, from files on its disk when it starts, and it checks the dashboard folder again while it runs.

Two small YAML files set it up. A data source file says where VictoriaMetrics is. A dashboard provider file names a folder on disk and the Grafana folder to show its dashboards in. With allowUiUpdates set to false, a person who edits a provisioned dashboard in the browser and presses Save gets the message "Cannot save provisioned dashboard". That is the point: the way to change a dashboard is a pull request that changes the JSON, reviewed like code.

code.text:
apiVersion: 1
providers:
  - name: lab
    folder: AI-Agents
    type: file
    updateIntervalSeconds: 10
    allowUiUpdates: false
    options:
      path: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards

notes.text: The Grafana folder these dashboards appear in.
How often Grafana looks for changed files. A saved edit to ops.json appears within seconds, with no restart.
Edits in the browser cannot be saved. The file stays the only source.
The folder inside the container. Docker mounts your dashboards/ folder here.

read.h: An alert is the same query, with a line and a clock
p: A dashboard only helps when someone looks at it. For the weekend we need the opposite: the database looks for us. An alert rule is a PromQL query with a condition, here the same cache-read share with < 0.70 at the end. A rule evaluator runs it again and again, every 15 seconds in the lab. With VictoriaMetrics that evaluator is a separate small program called vmalert; Prometheus has the same thing built in. Every series that the query returns is one alert, so if two agents lose their cache, two alerts start, each with its own agent label.

The for line adds the clock. When the condition first becomes true, the alert is only pending. It becomes firing only when the condition stayed true at every evaluation for the whole duration. That stops a single odd data point, such as one slow minute, from waking anyone. In the lab the rule waits 1 minute so you see it fire quickly; the real rule waits 2 hours, because a cache that recovers in ten minutes needs no person.

Labels and annotations travel with the alert. Labels, such as severity and service, are for machines: the next section uses them to decide who hears about it. Annotations are the text for people. {{ $labels.agent }} and {{ $value }} are filled in from the series that fired, so the message says which agent and how bad.

code.text:
groups:
  - name: ai-agents
    interval: 15s
    rules:
      - alert: AICacheReadShareLow
        expr: |
          sum by (agent) (rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{type="cache_read"}[1m]))
            / sum by (agent) (rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total[1m])) < 0.70
        for: 1m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          service: ai-agents
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.agent }} reads only {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its input from the prompt cache"

notes.text: How often vmalert runs every rule in this group.
The panel's query plus a condition. Only agents under 0.70 come back, and each one is an alert.
Pending first; firing only after a full minute under the line. The real rule uses 2h.
A routing label. Alertmanager will send everything with service=ai-agents to the alerts channel.
The human text, filled in per agent. humanizePercentage turns 0.15 into 15%.

deeper.h: Go deeper: alert on the forecast, not the total
p: Some alerts should come before the damage. Our spend rule compares the money spent so far this month with a straight line from zero to the monthly budget: on the 10th of a 30-day month, the line is at one third of the budget. When spend is more than 25% above that line for 6 hours, the rule fires, while there is still most of the month left to act. In PromQL the line is budget * day_of_month() / days_in_month().

Whatever an alert says, it only tells people. No alert pauses an agent, stops a run or scales anything down. Deciding what to do with the information stays with a person, because an alert built from a wrong number should never be able to stop real work.

read.h: From firing to a message in Slack
p: vmalert does not know Slack. When a rule fires, it sends the alert to Alertmanager, a separate program whose only job is to decide who hears about which alert, and how often. Its configuration is a tree of routes. Each route has matchers on labels and names a receiver; an alert goes to the first route whose matchers fit, and to the default receiver at the top when none fit. A receiver is a destination: in our platform a Slack channel, in the lab a small program on your laptop that prints what Slack would show.

A few settings keep the channel calm. group_by puts alerts with the same alert name and agent into one message. group_wait waits a few seconds before the first message, so alerts that start together arrive together. repeat_interval says how long to wait before reminding about an alert that is still firing. send_resolved sends one more message when the problem is gone, so nobody has to guess whether it was fixed.

code.text:
route:
  receiver: nobody
  group_by: [alertname, agent]
  group_wait: 10s
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - matchers: ['service="ai-agents"']
      receiver: ai-agents-alerts
receivers:
  - name: nobody
  - name: ai-agents-alerts
    slack_configs:
      - api_url_file: /etc/alertmanager/slack-webhook-url
        channel: "#ai-agents-alerts"
        title: '{{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}'
        send_resolved: true

notes.text: The default receiver. An alert whose labels match no route ends here, and nobody hears about it.
One message per alert name and agent, not one per evaluation.
The route: any alert with the label service="ai-agents" goes to the alerts channel.
The Slack webhook URL is a secret, so it is read from a file, not written in the config. The lab uses a webhook to your laptop instead.
Also send a message when the alert stops firing.

read.see:
#ai-agents-alerts  [FIRING] nova reads only 15% of its input from the prompt cache
#ai-agents-alerts  [RESOLVED] nova reads only 15% of its input from the prompt cache

lab.title: A dashboard from a file, and an alert that reaches Slack
needs: Docker Desktop running, with about 1.2 GB free for the images
lab.goal: Provision a Grafana dashboard from a JSON file, break a pretend agent's prompt cache, and watch an alert rule go from pending to firing to a message in a pretend Slack channel.

guess.q: The rule says share < 0.70 with for: 1m and runs every 15 seconds. Nova's cache breaks at 10:00. Because the rate looks back over one minute, the share drifts down and falls under 0.70 at about 10:01. When does the first Slack message appear?

options.text: At about 10:01, as soon as the share is under the line
options.why: At that moment the alert is only pending. It fires only after the condition held for the whole minute.

options.text: A little after 10:02: one minute pending, then firing, then Alertmanager's short group wait
options.why: The for duration starts when the condition first holds, and Alertmanager waits group_wait (10 seconds here) before it sends the first message.

options.text: Never, unless someone has the dashboard open
options.why: Rules and dashboards are separate. vmalert evaluates the rule whether or not anyone looks at Grafana.

follow.say: Make a lab folder with two small Node programs and no packages to install. The first pretends to be the gateway: it counts tokens and dollars for Nova and the CI fixer, and /break makes Nova's cache stop working. The second pretends to be Slack and prints every message it receives.
Leave the gateway running. In a second tab start the pretend Slack and leave it open too, because this is where the alert will appear.

In a third tab, write the three configuration files from the lesson: what VictoriaMetrics scrapes, the alert rule, and Alertmanager's route to the pretend Slack. The route sets group_interval to 30 seconds, so the resolved message comes quickly; the default is 5 minutes.
follow.do:
cd ~/academy-labs/p6-3
cat > scrape.yml <<'EOF'
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: gateway
    scrape_interval: 10s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["host.docker.internal:9464"]
EOF
cat > rules.yml <<'EOF'
groups:
  - name: ai-agents
    interval: 15s
    rules:
      - alert: AICacheReadShareLow
        expr: |
          sum by (agent) (rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{type="cache_read"}[1m]))
            / sum by (agent) (rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total[1m])) < 0.70
        for: 1m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          service: ai-agents
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.agent }} reads only {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its input from the prompt cache"
EOF
cat > alertmanager.yml <<'EOF'
route:
  receiver: nobody
  group_by: [alertname, agent]
  group_wait: 10s
  group_interval: 30s
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - matchers: ['service="ai-agents"']
      receiver: ai-agents-alerts
receivers:
  - name: nobody
  - name: ai-agents-alerts
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://host.docker.internal:5001/
        send_resolved: true
EOF
docker run --rm -v "$PWD/rules.yml:/rules.yml" victoriametrics/vmalert:v1.154.0 -rule=/rules.yml -dryRun 2>&1 | grep -E 'finished reading|error'

groups:

explain: The cache-read panel and AICacheReadShareLow use the same expression. What does each one add to it, and why do we need both?
Why does the real rule wait for 2h before it fires, and what would happen in the channel with no for at all?
Why are dashboards provisioned from JSON files in git instead of saved in the Grafana UI?

check.q: Nova's cache-read share panel turns red at 02:00 on a Sunday. What makes sure a person hears about it?

options.text: The red threshold colour on the stat panel
options.why: A colour only helps someone who is looking. At 02:00 on a Sunday nobody is.

options.text: Setting the dashboard to refresh every 10 seconds
options.why: Refresh redraws the panel for whoever has it open. It sends nothing to anyone.

options.text: An alert rule with the same expression, a condition and a for duration, routed by Alertmanager to the alerts channel
options.why: The rule is evaluated whether or not anyone looks, and Alertmanager delivers the message to people.

check.q: Why does the real cache-read rule have for: 2h instead of firing at the first low value?

options.text: So that a short dip that fixes itself does not wake anyone; only a problem that lasts reaches people
options.why: The alert stays pending while the condition holds and fires only after two hours. A cache that recovers in ten minutes needs no person.

options.text: Because vmalert can only evaluate a rule every two hours
options.why: The group's interval sets how often the rule runs, for example every hour or every 15 seconds. for is a separate setting about how long the condition must hold.

options.text: To give Grafana time to draw the panel first
options.why: Rules do not depend on Grafana at all. vmalert asks VictoriaMetrics directly.

check.q: The spend alert fires: Nova is more than 25% ahead of its monthly budget line. What happens to Nova's runs?

options.text: The gateway refuses Nova's model calls until the next month
options.why: No alert stops anything. An alert built from a wrong number must never be able to stop real work.

options.text: Nothing changes in the runs; people get a message with a link to the spend dashboard and decide what to do
options.why: Alerts tell people. The decision stays with a person, who can read the dashboard and find the cause.

options.text: Alertmanager pauses Nova's schedule until someone silences the alert
options.why: Alertmanager only sends messages. It has no way to reach the agents, and we would not want it to.

p: Our dashboards are JSON files in the infrastructure repo under modules/grafana/dashboards/AI-Agents/. On inf, a sidecar container next to Grafana loads every file in that folder, and the folder name becomes the Grafana folder, so a dashboard change is a pull request. The operations dashboard shows cost and tokens per agent from the gateway's counters, the cache-read share in red under 70%, and two log panels from VictoriaLogs: API errors and tool calls a hook refused. No dashboard has a person variable; the dropdowns are agent, team, suite and split.

The alert rules live next to the other VictoriaMetrics rules in the infrastructure repo, in ai-spend.yml. AISpendAheadOfBudget fires when month-to-date spend is more than 25% ahead of a straight line to the monthly budget for 6 hours, per scope (people, and each agent); AICacheReadShareLow fires when an agent's cache-read share stays under 70% for 2 hours. Both copy the label set the existing routes expect, so they reach #ai-agents-alerts and mention Sean and Nir. The eval scoreboard and the delivery dashboard reuse the same mechanics: variables, one query per panel, files in git.

tickets.why: The operations dashboard: cost, tokens, cache-read share, API errors and refused tool calls, as a provisioned JSON file.
The spend view and its two rules, the burn-rate forecast and the low cache-read share, routed to the alerts channel.
The eval scoreboard: a panel repeated per suite with a pass-rate band, the same panel and variable mechanics.
The delivery dashboard: team variable only, baseline lines, and throughput always next to change failure.

words.plain: One chart on a Grafana dashboard: a type, a position on the grid, and one or more queries.
A dropdown such as $agent that Grafana replaces in every query before sending it.
Grafana loading dashboards and data sources from files on disk, so they can live in git.
A query with a condition that a rule evaluator runs on a timer; every series it returns is one alert.
The state of an alert whose condition is true but has not yet held for the whole for duration.
The program that receives firing alerts and routes them by their labels to receivers such as a Slack channel.

review.q: Write the alert rule for "an agent's cache-read share under 70% for 2 hours" from memory: the expression, for, and the labels it needs.
review.a: The panel's ratio of sum by (agent) rate of cache_read tokens to sum by (agent) rate of all input tokens, < 0.70, for: 2h, and the routing labels the Alertmanager route matches (in the lab, service: ai-agents).

review.q: An alert fires in vmalert but never reaches Slack. Name the two places you check and what you look for.
review.a: Alertmanager's alerts list, to see which receiver the alert went to, and the alert's labels against the route's matchers. A label typo sends it to the default receiver.

review.q: Why keep dashboards as files in git, and what does allowUiUpdates: false do?
review.a: Every change is reviewed and can be reverted, and every Grafana gets the same dashboards. With allowUiUpdates false, saving a provisioned dashboard in the browser is refused, so the file stays the only source.

remember: A panel is a saved query that someone has to look at; an alert rule is the same query with a line and a clock that finds people by itself, and it only ever tells them.
